transcript.content: Hi, welcome in. I'm Dr. [Name], one of the psychiatrists here. To start, can you tell me what's been bringing you in to see me today?

Well, I’m here because people keep telling me it’s just foreclosure paperwork, like I missed this or didn’t sign that, but that’s not what’s actually happening. The bank and the loan servicer have been coordinating things, and I’m pretty sure people at my job are involved too. I supervise retail sales, so I know when people are whispering and pretending they aren’t—customers do it too sometimes, but that’s different.

This has been going on for almost two years, with the house. They keep showing me papers like that’s supposed to prove something, but papers can be arranged. I know what I’ve been seeing. It feels like they’re all trying to push me out of my home and make it look like it’s my fault.

Over these past two years, have you noticed extended periods—weeks at a time—where your mood was very low or, alternatively, unusually high, energetic, or irritable, separate from how you feel about the situation with your house?

I mean... I don’t know. Low, high—those are kind of vague, you know? I’ve been stressed, obviously, because when you’re dealing with a house and people acting like paperwork is the whole story, that gets to you.

But weeks where I’m just, like, a totally different mood for no reason? I haven’t really thought of it that way. At work I still have to open the store, handle schedules, deal with returns—people get very dramatic about returns, honestly, like last week this woman tried to bring back something that had clearly been worn. So I don’t know if that counts as irritable or just normal.

I guess I’d say I haven’t noticed anything separate from all this house situation. It’s hard to separate it.
Have you ever heard voices or sounds that other people couldn't hear, or sensed things—like smells, feelings of being touched, or seeing things—that others around you didn't notice?

I don’t think so. I mean, sometimes I hear people talking low, like at work or outside the house, and I can’t always make out what they’re saying—but that’s just people talking, you know? Retail stores are noisy, there’s music, carts, the register beeping, somebody asking where the socks are when there’s a giant sign right there.

But voices that nobody else could hear… I’m not sure what that would be like. I haven’t noticed smells or being touched or seeing things that other people don’t see. At least not in the way you’re asking, I don’t think.
Aside from the situation with your house, have you noticed any changes in how you're managing at work, taking care of yourself, or spending time with friends and family over the past two years?

Mostly I’m still functioning, if that’s what you mean. Like, I get up, I go to work, I supervise my team, I do the schedules, deal with customers complaining about prices or returns or whatever. I still shower, get dressed, handle my basic stuff.

It’s more when something connects back to the house—like mail from the bank, phone calls, paperwork at work that seems… off, or like it’s being arranged somehow—that’s when I get thrown. Because then it’s not just “work paperwork,” it feels tied into the whole thing. Otherwise, if the foreclosure stuff isn’t in my face, I can do what I need to do.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient exhibits a fixed, non-bizarre persecutory delusion (belief that the bank, loan servicer, and coworkers are conspiring to force him out of his home via falsified paperwork) that has persisted for approximately two years. There are no hallucinations, no disorganized speech/behavior, and no sustained mood episode (manic or depressive) independent of the delusional content. Functioning is largely preserved outside of delusion-related triggers, with intact self-care, work performance, and social role functioning. This clinical picture—an isolated, persistent delusion without other psychotic features, mood syndrome, or significant functional decline—is most consistent with Delusional Disorder, persecutory type (F22), rather than Schizophrenia (which requires additional psychotic symptoms and more pervasive functional impairment) or a mood disorder with psychotic features (no manic/depressive episode identified).
